title: The Orchard of Nagasaki's harbor
premise: In the winter of 1945, Ada Okafor, a Nigerian-born nurse stationed near Nagasaki's ruined harbor, keeps a secret ledger recording the names of the dead that military reports omit. When the season's last bridge closes, she is trapped in a coastal village with Kenji Mori, a lacquerware artisan whose family workshop holds a centuries-old orchard of grafted trees — and whose brother's name appears in her ledger under circumstances the army wants buried. As occupation officers move to demolish the workshop for a supply depot, Ada and Kenji race to finish his father's final commission: a memorial chest bearing every name she has recorded. The book ends with the bridge reopening in spring; Ada chooses to stay through one more harvest, mailing the finished chest to the families while choosing love over the repatriation orders that would carry her away.
about_author: Edmund Hartwell is the pen name of a former merchant-marine radio operator who spent three years in postwar Japanese ports and never stopped writing letters home about what he saw there. He lives in Cornwall, where he grafts apple trees descended from cuttings he carried back in 1949.

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. In a requisitioned schoolhouse hospital, Ada tends burn victims and secretly records names the officers' reports omit, pressing each entry into a small ledger she carries against her ribs. When evacuation orders list the harbor villages for closure, she realizes the ledger may be the only record some families ever receive. Emotional beat: quiet defiance born of grief.

chapters.title: Last Crossing
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Racing to reach the coastal clinic before winter, Ada arrives at the bridge as soldiers seal it for the season. Stranded in the village of Tomioka, she is taken in by Kenji Mori, a lacquer artisan working alone in his family's workshop beneath an orchard of ancient grafted trees. Emotional beat: reluctant shelter, first wary connection.

chapters.title: The Lacquerer's Hands
chapters.summary: Kenji's POV. Kenji resents the foreign nurse billeted in his home but watches her kneel to wash his dying father's hands with the same care she gives everything. He reveals the workshop's purpose: his father's unfinished memorial chest, meant to hold the names of the village dead. Emotional beat: grief finding a shared language in craft.

chapters.title: What the Orchard Remembers
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Walking the terraced orchard, Ada learns each tree was grafted from a cutting brought by a different generation of Mori women, a living archive older than any paper record. She shows Kenji her ledger; he recognizes his brother Hideo's name among the omitted dead. Emotional beat: two archives — wood and ink — recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Requisition
chapters.summary: Kenji's POV. Occupation officer Captain Bellamy arrives with demolition orders: the workshop stands on ground needed for a fuel depot. Kenji bargains for thirty days to finish the chest, offering his father's prized lacquer collection as collateral. Bellamy, himself haunted by a name he cannot say aloud, grants it coldly. Emotional beat: time becoming a currency.

chapters.title: Thirty Days of Winter
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Ada and Kenji work by lamplight — she transcribing names onto paper slips, he sealing them beneath layers of urushi lacquer. Villagers bring scraps of cloth, letters, hair ribbons to include. An air raid siren's false alarm nearly destroys the drying chest. Emotional beat: a community building its own monument.

chapters.title: Bellamy's Ledger
chapters.summary: Bellamy's POV. Inspecting the work, Bellamy finds his own war dead recorded in Ada's pages — men whose deaths he signed off and was ordered to forget. He confronts Ada at night, half threat, half confession. She offers him no absolution, only a blank page and a pen. Emotional beat: the enemy revealed as another keeper of omissions.

chapters.title: The Name That Was Cut
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada discovers why Hideo's death was expunged: he died shielding Korean conscript laborers from a guard, an act the reports could not accommodate. Kenji, shattered, wants to carve the truth into the chest's lid regardless of consequence. Ada must choose between protecting him and protecting the record. Emotional beat: love tested against duty to the dead.

chapters.title: Demolition Day
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating POVs. Bellamy's crews arrive early. Kenji refuses to leave the chest; Ada stands between the bulldozer and the orchard, reading names aloud until the workers falter. Bellamy halts the demolition, reclassifying the workshop as a 'memorial site,' at cost to his career. The final layer of lacquer dries that night. Emotional beat: witness as resistance; the record survives.

chapters.title: Spring Crossing
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The bridge reopens with the thaw. Repatriation papers offer Ada passage home; instead she mails the finished chest to the families, plants a new grafting in the orchard, and asks Kenji to teach her the lacquerer's patience. The last entry in her ledger is not a death but a beginning. Emotional beat: inheritance chosen freely; memory taking root.
